chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
title: Columbia's free hand and the Sinatra-level publicity deal
summary: Columbia, under Manny Sachs, gave him freedom; he asked for the same publicity as Sinatra and Dinah Shore rather than money.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Was there a particular attitude by Columbia that started to happen with the kind of music that you were quite successful with?
They gave us a very free hand.

Very. And, of course, I was there during a period which was not a long one, where a guy -- Manny Sachs, who was Sinatra's man, and he liked music and he had a flare for putting good things together. And very few suggestions, other than, 'Can I do something for you?'
What was the mode of promotions at that time, as you look back?
Well, the mode of promotion in our case was the only smart business arrangement I ever did in my life,

probably. And I don't think you can call it a business arrangement, but I'm pretty sure that there were a lot of my contemporaries, particularly those on Columbia, who never knew at the time what was happening.

My idea with Columbia Records was not how much money or how many pressings or any of the things that I knew were pretty difficult in the wartime, because there were too many limitations in the situation. So what I did ask Mr. Sachs for was the same amount of exploitation, publicity and press, -- whatever you want to call it, advertising, that their top two stars, their top two people -- and their top two people were, to the best of my recollection, Frank Sinatra and Dinah Shore.

And every time there was an ad in Variety or Billboard or any other kind of exploitation, I had it. And I'm sure that Les Brown, Harry James, and everybody else there was wondering, many times, 'What the hell is going on?'
Yeah, there were a lot of other bands on the same label, Charlie Spivak --
